title: vpseasy
text:
A VPS (virtual private server) is a small Linux machine you rent from a cloud provider. Getting one ready for an app means the same chores every time. You create the server, add a user who logs in with your SSH key, turn off password logins, install Docker, copy your app over and start it. vpseasy does each chore with one function call, and vps_deploy does all of them in order.
The setup of a new server is written down in a cloud-init file. Cloud-init is the program that Ubuntu cloud images run on their first boot. It reads a YAML file supplied when the server is created, and from it installs packages, creates users and runs commands. vpseasy writes that file for you.
You can try the file on your own computer before paying for a server. Multipass starts Ubuntu virtual machines locally and accepts the same cloud-init file, so a mistake in the setup shows up on your laptop in a few minutes rather than on a live server.
Once a server is up, vpseasy copies your app directory to it with rsync and runs docker compose up. It can also write the Compose file for a common layout, with the app behind the Caddy web server and a Cloudflare tunnel, and add Litestream to back up SQLite databases to a storage bucket.

title: vpseasy
text:
Install
pip install vpseasy            # Hetzner and Multipass
pip install 'vpseasy[aws]'     # adds boto3 for Lightsail
Hetzner needs an API token in HCLOUD_TOKEN. Lightsail uses your normal AWS credentials, for example AWS_PROFILE. Multipass is installed separately and must be on your PATH.

title: vpseasy
text:
Cloud-init
Two functions write a cloud-init file, one for each kind of machine. Both create a user called deploy who can use sudo without a password and can log in only with the SSH keys you pass. Both turn off root and password logins, and both install Docker unless you pass docker=False. Each returns the YAML text as yaml and the path of the matching private key as key.
multi_init is for a local Multipass VM and keeps the setup small so the VM starts quickly. Here docker=False also skips the reboot that follows a Docker install:

_vm = 'testvm'
mi = multi_init(_vm, ['ssh-ed25519 AAAA... me'], docker=False)   # omit pub_keys to generate ~/.ssh/testvm; docker=False is faster locally
print(mi.yaml)

#cloud-config
hostname: testvm
preserve_hostname: false
packages:
- curl
package_update: true
package_upgrade: true
disable_root: true
ssh_pwauth: false
users:
- name: deploy
  groups:
  - sudo
  shell: /bin/bash
  sudo:
  - ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL
  ssh_authorized_keys:
  - ssh-ed25519 AAAA... me



vps_init is for a real server on the internet, so it adds protection. It installs fail2ban, which blocks addresses that keep failing to log in, and unattended-upgrades, which applies security updates by itself. It turns on the UFW firewall with only SSH (port 22) allowed, sets up log rotation and reboots once setup is done. It also adds a 4 GB swap file with a low swappiness, so a memory spike slows the server down instead of killing a container; swap=None leaves swap out. Extra packages go in pkgs and extra shell commands in cmds.
If you leave out pub_keys, either function generates a new key pair at ~/.ssh/<hostname>, replacing any key already there, and returns its path as key. The other functions find that key when you give them the server’s name, so this is the simplest way to start. When you pass your own public keys, key is None.

ci = vps_init('demo-prod', ['ssh-ed25519 AAAA... me'])   # omit pub_keys to generate ~/.ssh/demo-prod
print(ci.yaml)

Local testing with Multipass
Multipass wraps the multipass command. Its launch method starts a VM and hands it the cloud-init file; pass it the object that multi_init or vps_init returned. The VM gets its own IP address on your machine, and ip returns it. A Docker install inside the VM adds about two minutes, for the install and the reboot after it.
The next cell makes a tiny app to deploy: a directory that holds only a docker-compose.yml running nginx.

import tempfile
_app = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / 'myapp'
_app.mkdir()
(_app / 'docker-compose.yml').write_text('services:\n  app:\n    image: nginx:alpine\n')

41



mp = Multipass()
try: mp.rm(_vm, purge=True)
except: pass
vm = mp.launch(_vm, image='24.04', cpus=1, memory='1G', disk='10G', cloud_init=mi)
ip = mp.ip(vm.name)
print(f'VM at {ip}, key: {vm.key}')

title: vpseasy
text:
Provision and deploy on Hetzner
Hetzner Cloud rents VPSes in Europe and the US. Set HCLOUD_TOKEN to an API token from its console. hetzner_deploy runs vps_deploy with a Hetzner provider and Hetzner’s defaults, Ubuntu 24.04 on a cx23 server.
vps_deploy does the whole job. If no server with that name exists, it creates one from a vps_init file with a new key pair at ~/.ssh/<name>. It then waits for SSH and for cloud-init to finish, copies src to /srv/app and runs docker compose up -d --build. If the server already exists, it skips the creation and logs in with the key at ~/.ssh/<name>, so running it again deploys your new code to the same server. It returns the server’s IP address, name and key path.
Each deploy keeps the images it builds, tagged with their build time, and deletes dangling images and build cache afterwards. If a new build misbehaves, rollback(ip) puts the previous image back and restarts the app; rollback(ip, 'prev') reverses that. It restores the image only, not the copied files or the data. wait_http waits until the site answers after a deploy, and server_health reports memory, swap, load, disk and each container.
Hetzner.servers lists your servers and Hetzner.delete removes one by name, as the second cell shows.

hz = Hetzner()
svr = hetzner_deploy('myapp-prod',_app, hz) # hz is not required

title: vpseasy
text:
Lightsail
Lightsail is Amazon’s fixed-price VPS service. Install the extra with pip install 'vpseasy[aws]' and make AWS credentials available in any of the usual ways, such as AWS_PROFILE. The region defaults to Sydney (ap-southeast-2); pass region= to Lightsail to change it.
Lightsail has the same methods as Hetzner, so vps_deploy accepts either. Keyword arguments that vps_deploy does not know go to create, which is how bundle= below picks the instance size. Lightsail’s create does more than Hetzner’s. It leaves an existing instance alone instead of failing, gives the instance a static IP address that stays the same when it restarts, closes every public port except SSH, and turns on a daily snapshot at 16:00 UTC. ports= and snapshots= change the last two. SSH alone is enough when web traffic arrives through a Cloudflare tunnel, as in the Compose layout further down.

ls = Lightsail()
r = vps_deploy('lh', _app, ls, bundle='small_3_2')
print(f'Deployed at {r.ip}, key: {r.key}')

Lightsail does not read cloud-init YAML. It runs the user data you give it as a shell script, so create converts the vps_init file with cloud_init_sh. The result is a bash script that does the same work: it sets the hostname, creates the users with their sudo rules and SSH keys, writes files, installs packages and runs the commands. It does not reboot. At the end it creates /var/lib/vpseasy/ready, or /var/lib/vpseasy/error if a step failed, and wait_ready watches for those files. Here is the start of a converted script:

ud = cloud_init_sh(vps_init('demo', ['ssh-ed25519 AAAA... demo']).yaml)
print(ud[ud.index('hostnamectl'):][:600])

hostnamectl set-hostname demo
echo 'PasswordAuthentication no' > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-vpseasy.conf
id -u deploy >/dev/null 2>&1 || useradd -m -s /bin/bash deploy
usermod -aG sudo deploy
cat > /etc/sudoers.d/90-vpseasy-deploy <<'VPSEASY_EOF'
deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL
VPSEASY_EOF
chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/90-vpseasy-deploy
install -d -m 700 -o deploy -g deploy /home/deploy/.ssh
cat > /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys <<'VPSEASY_EOF'
ssh-ed25519 AAAA... demo
VPSEASY_EOF
chown deploy:deploy /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys
mkdir -p /etc/logrotat

title: vpseasy
text:
Docker Compose helpers
Docker Compose runs several containers together from one docker-compose.yml file. A small web app behind a Cloudflare tunnel usually needs the same pieces. There is the app container, Caddy as the web server in front of it, and a cloudflared container that keeps the tunnel to Cloudflare open, all on a shared network called web. Caddy also needs two named volumes for its certificates and settings. The app is built from a Dockerfile made with dockeasy, which has recipes for FastHTML and other Python apps, Go, Rust and Node.
caddy_stack writes all of this from a domain name and a dockeasy Dockerfile object. It saves three files into root: Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml and Caddyfile. If you leave out root, they are written to the current directory. It returns the Compose object, which prints as YAML.
vols lists directories inside the container whose contents should stay on the server’s disk when the container is rebuilt. vols_to_binds turns each one into a bind mount from a folder of the same name next to the Compose file, so /app/data becomes ./data:/app/data. The app reads its settings and secrets from .env, and the cloudflared container takes its tunnel token from the CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN variable. Pass cloudflared=False to leave out the tunnel and have Caddy listen on ports 80 and 443 itself.

d = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
df = fasthtml_app(pkgs=['sqlite3'], vols=['/app/data'], healthcheck='/health')
c = caddy_stack('myapp.example.com', df, vols=['/app/data'], root=d)
print(c)

services:
  app:
    build: .
    volumes:
    - ./data:/app/data
    env_file:
    - .env
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
    - web
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2
    depends_on:
    - app
    volumes:
    - /private/var/folders/kg/9vdw4mdd1fs58svgh4k1qhr09x7dqh/T/tmpfs6cqxh2/Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
    - caddy_data:/data
    - caddy_config:/config
    networks:
    - web
    restart: unless-stopped
  cloudflared:
    image: cloudflare/cloudflared:latest
    command: tunnel --no-autoupdate run --url http://caddy
    environment:
    - TUNNEL_TOKEN=${CF_TUNNEL_TOKEN}
    networks:
    - web
    restart: unless-stopped
networks:
  web: null
volumes:
  caddy_data: null
  caddy_config: null

title: vpseasy
text:
Litestream backups
SQLite keeps a whole database in one file, which is convenient until the server is lost and the file with it. Litestream runs beside the app, copies every change into an S3-compatible storage bucket, and can rebuild the file from there. The bucket can be a Lightsail bucket, AWS S3 or Cloudflare R2. For R2, use endpoint='https://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com' and region='auto'.
Lightsail.bucket creates a Lightsail bucket if it does not exist and makes a new access key for it. Put the key in .env as LITESTREAM_ACCESS_KEY_ID and LITESTREAM_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. Copy the secret straight away, because Lightsail shows it only once. A bucket can have only two access keys, so a third call fails until you delete one.

b = Lightsail().bucket('lh-backups')
b.bucket, b.endpoint, b.key_id

litestream_conf writes the Litestream config file, litestream.yml, and returns its text. The database paths are paths inside the container, so they must sit under one of the app’s volumes. Each database is stored at <prefix>/<db path> in the bucket, which keeps two databases with the same file name apart. By default Litestream takes a full snapshot every 24 hours and keeps 72 hours of history; snapshot= and retention= change that.

d = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
print(litestream_conf(['/app/data/app.db'], 'lh-backups', endpoint='https://s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com',
                      region='ap-southeast-2', prefix='lh', conf=d/'litestream.yml'))

snapshot:
  interval: 24h
  retention: 72h
validation:
  interval: 12h
dbs:
- path: /app/data/app.db
  replica:
    type: s3
    bucket: lh-backups
    path: lh/app/data/app.db
    region: ap-southeast-2
    access-key-id: ${LITESTREAM_ACCESS_KEY_ID}
    secret-access-key: ${LITESTREAM_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}
    endpoint: https://s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com



You will usually pass the same settings to caddy_stack as litestream=dict(...) and let it write the config. It adds two services. litestream-restore runs once at startup and restores the database from the bucket when the file is missing and a copy exists. The app does not start until it has finished, so a brand new server gets its data back before the app can create an empty database. The litestream service starts after the app and keeps copying changes. With several databases there is one restore service for each. The output shows how the three services depend on each other:

c = caddy_stack('lh.example.com', fasthtml_app(vols=['/app/data']), vols=['/app/data'], root=d,
                litestream=dict(dbs=['/app/data/app.db'], bucket='lh-backups', region='ap-southeast-2', prefix='lh',
                                endpoint='https://s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com'))
svcs = c.to_dict()['services']
print(yaml.safe_dump({k: {o: v[o] for o in ('image', 'command', 'depends_on', 'restart') if o in v} for k,v in svcs.items()
                      if k in ('app', 'litestream-restore', 'litestream')}, sort_keys=False))

app:
  depends_on:
    litestream-restore:
      condition: service_completed_successfully
  restart: unless-stopped
litestream-restore:
  image: litestream/litestream:0.5
  command: restore -if-db-not-exists -if-replica-exists /app/data/app.db
  restart: 'no'
litestream:
  image: litestream/litestream:0.5
  command: replicate
  depends_on:
  - app
  restart: unless-stopped

title: core
text:
Multipass runs Ubuntu virtual machines on your own computer. Testing a cloud-init file and a deploy on one costs nothing and takes a few minutes, so it is worth doing before you create a real server. Install Multipass and make sure the multipass command is on your PATH.
Multipass wraps that command. launch starts a VM, optionally with a cloud-init file from multi_init or vps_init and with host folders mounted inside it (mounts={host_path: vm_path}). vms lists VM names, ip gives a VM’s address, exec_ runs a command inside it and rm deletes it. Any other subcommand works as a method too, so mp.info('testvm') runs multipass info testvm. The module creates one instance for you as mp.

text:
Cloud-init generation
A new cloud server starts as a bare Ubuntu image. Cloud-init is the program that runs on its first boot and sets it up from a YAML file supplied when the server is created: it installs packages, creates users, adds SSH keys and runs commands. The two functions here write that file. Both return an AttrDict with the YAML text as yaml and the path of the matching private key as key.
vps_init is for a public server, on Hetzner or Lightsail. It builds the file with fastcloudinit’s cloud_init_config, which turns on the UFW firewall with only SSH allowed, adds log rotation and reboots at the end. vpseasy adds the fail2ban and unattended-upgrades packages and, unless docker=False, installs Docker and puts the user in the docker group. Other keyword arguments go to cloud_init_config.
multi_init is for a Multipass VM. It uses the smaller cloud_init_base, with the same user and Docker setup but no firewall and no fail2ban, so the VM boots faster. It reboots only when there are commands to run, and the Docker install counts as commands.
Both create one user, deploy by default, who can use sudo without a password and logs in only with the SSH keys in pub_keys. If pub_keys is left out, gen_key makes a new ed25519 key pair at ~/.ssh/<hostname>, replacing any key already there, and key points at it. Otherwise key is None. Extra packages go in pkgs and extra shell commands in cmds; the commands run after the Docker install.
vps_init also adds a swap file, 4 GB by default, and sets the kernel’s swappiness to 10, so the server swaps only under real memory pressure. A small server running several containers would otherwise kill a process when memory runs out. Pass swap=None to leave swap alone, or another size such as swap='2G'. swap_cmds returns those commands on their own, for a server that already exists.
The first test below passes a key, so none is generated. The second generates one and deletes it again.

Hetzner
Hetzner manages servers on Hetzner Cloud through the hcloud Python SDK, so you do not need Hetzner’s command-line tool or a config file. It reads the API token from HCLOUD_TOKEN unless you pass token=, and raises ValueError if there is none.
create makes a server and returns its IP address, name, key path and the raw SDK response. Give it the result of vps_init as cloud_init, and the key path comes back with the server. ssh_keys is a different way to log in. It names keys stored in your Hetzner account, and Hetzner adds them to the root user only. They give no access to the deploy user that cloud-init creates, so create refuses to take both. key_names lists the stored keys for that purpose.
servers lists your servers with their IP and status, get returns one by name or None, server_ip returns its address and delete removes it. Deleting a server that does not exist does nothing.

title: core
text:
Lightsail
Lightsail is Amazon’s fixed-price VPS service. Lightsail has the same methods as Hetzner (servers, get, server_ip, create and delete) and talks to AWS through boto3, so vps_deploy works with either. boto3 is an optional extra: pip install 'vpseasy[aws]'. Credentials come from the standard AWS chain, for example an SSO profile named in AWS_PROFILE or passed as profile=. The region defaults to ap-southeast-2 (Sydney).
create is safe to run twice: an instance that already exists is not created again. Either way it waits until the instance is running, attaches a static IP address named <name>-ip, sets the open public ports to ports and turns on a daily automatic snapshot at snapshots. By default only SSH is open, since web traffic arrives through the Cloudflare tunnel, and the snapshot is taken at 16:00 UTC. delete removes the instance and releases its static IP. bucket makes a storage bucket for backups and is covered with Litestream below.
Lightsail runs user data as a shell script and does not read cloud-config YAML, so create converts a vps_init file with cloud_init_sh. The script sets the hostname, turns off password logins, creates the users with their groups, sudo rules and SSH keys, writes files, applies apt settings, installs packages and runs the commands, in that order. It does not reboot. It keeps the original YAML in /var/lib/vpseasy/cloud-config.yaml and logs to /var/log/vpseasy-init.log. When it finishes it creates /var/lib/vpseasy/ready, or /var/lib/vpseasy/error if a step failed, and chk_cloud_init reads those files. cloud_init_sh raises ValueError for any cloud-config key it cannot convert. Running cloud-init itself on the YAML in /etc/cloud/cloud.cfg.d was tried on Ubuntu 24.04 and did not create the users, which is why the conversion exists.

text:
SSH helpers
These functions call the system ssh and rsync commands, so there is no Python SSH library to install. They share a few arguments. user (or u) is the login name, deploy by default. The private key is found in this order: the path in key (or k); then ~/.ssh/<name> if you pass name, which raises FileNotFoundError when no file is there; then whatever ssh would use by itself. key_pass is the passphrase of an encrypted key and password is a login password for servers that accept one. Pass True to either to be asked for it. The first connection to a new host adds it to known_hosts without asking.
run_ssh runs one or more commands on the host, joined with &&, and returns their output, with anything written to stderr appended after ;;. If a command fails it raises IOError, unless you pass check=False, in which case it returns (exit code, output). stdin_data is sent to the remote command’s standard input.
sync copies a local directory to path on the host with rsync. It first creates path with sudo if it is missing or not writable. It deletes remote files that are not in src, so point it at a directory that belongs to the app alone. exclude skips files that match a pattern. include works the other way round: only matching files are copied, and a pattern ending in / takes a whole directory. extra adds rsync flags such as --checksum.
sync raises CalledProcessError when rsync fails, so nothing runs on a half-copied folder; with check=False it returns rsync’s exit code instead.
sync_paths copies chosen paths rather than a whole folder, for content that changes without a rebuild, such as the files behind a bind mount. Each path under src goes to the same path under path, with one rsync per path, so --delete removes only files inside that path and never reaches the rest of the server’s folder. A path missing from src is skipped, and rsync’s --mkpath creates missing remote folders. last names a pattern held back from a first pass and sent in a second one. Use it when something on the server watches for one kind of file, so that the files beside it land first: with last='*.json', an audio file is in place before the JSON that names it. A path that names the folder itself, such as ., '' or /, or one that resolves to it or leaves it, through .. or a symlink, raises ValueError, since its --delete would reach the whole folder. dry_run=True lists the changes without making them, and with host=None the copy goes to a local folder, which is handy for tests. rsync_cmds returns the commands without running them.
deploy runs sync, then docker compose up -d --remove-orphans in path, adding --build unless build=False. It starts Compose only if Docker works for the user and path holds a docker-compose.yml; otherwise it stops after copying. chk_docker is that Docker check on its own and returns True or False. After a build, deploy keeps the new image and the one it replaced with keep_image, so rollback can return to either; keep=0 turns that off. After the build, prune=True deletes dangling images and the build cache, which otherwise grow by the size of an image on every deploy. Kept images carry tags, so pruning leaves them.
ssh_cmd, res_key and askpass_env are the pieces these functions share: the ssh command line, the key lookup, and a context manager that answers a password prompt. They are public for callers that run their own ssh or rsync. Every function that connects takes port, for servers whose SSH listens somewhere other than 22.

Verification helpers
create returns as soon as the provider accepts the request, while the server is still booting and cloud-init is still working. Copying files at that point fails or races the setup, so these functions wait.
wait_ssh tries a trivial SSH command every interval seconds until it succeeds, and raises TimeoutError after tout seconds. chk_cloud_init asks once whether setup has finished and returns done, running or error. On a server set up by a cloud_init_sh script it reads that script’s marker files in /var/lib/vpseasy. Elsewhere it checks for /var/lib/cloud/instance/boot-finished, the file cloud-init writes when it is done. It returns unknown if the command printed nothing. wait_ready, further down, runs both in a loop.

wait_ready waits for SSH with wait_ssh, then calls chk_cloud_init every interval seconds until it says done. It raises RuntimeError if setup reports an error. A slow server gets retries extra rounds of tout seconds each, with a message printed before each one, and then TimeoutError is raised.
vps_deploy is the function most people want. It takes a server name, a local directory and a provider such as Hetzner() or Lightsail(). If the provider has no server by that name, vps_deploy creates one from vps_init(name), which makes a new key pair at ~/.ssh/<name>, and removes any old known_hosts entry for the new IP address. If the server exists, it uses the key at ~/.ssh/<name>, or key if you give one. Either way it then runs wait_ready and deploy, and returns the IP address, name and key path. Extra keyword arguments go to the provider’s create, for example server_type= for Hetzner or bundle= for Lightsail. Because it checks before creating, running it again redeploys to the same server.
hetzner_deploy is vps_deploy with a Hetzner provider and Hetzner’s image, server_type and location arguments. It remains for code written before Lightsail support.

title: core
text:
Rollback
A deploy builds a new image and replaces the running container, and a bad build takes the site down with it. deploy therefore keeps the image it replaces, and rollback puts it back.
Compose names the image it builds for a service after the project folder and the service, so /srv/app with service app builds app-app:latest. Compose strips characters other than lower-case letters, digits, - and _ from the folder name, and so does vpseasy. Pass img when the project is named otherwise, by a name: in the Compose file or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME; vps_deploy passes it on to deploy. A failed docker rmi, for a tag a stopped container still uses, leaves the tag and does not stop the deploy. After each build, keep_image tags the new image with its build time in UTC, such as app-app:20261019T063000, and tags the image that ran before it app-app:prev, also giving that one its build time when it has none. It then deletes the timestamped tags past the newest keep by build time, three by default, except the running image’s and prev’s. An image with two timestamps counts once, and a build whose second another build already holds takes the next free second. deploy runs keep_image even when the restart after a build fails, since the new build already holds latest. Every build keeps its tag until it falls out of the newest keep, whatever rollbacks happen in between, so no build loses its last tag while it is still among them. Pruning after the build deletes only dangling images, so the kept ones stay. kept_images lists the kept tags, newest first, with their image IDs.
rollback points the service at a kept image and restarts it. Without to, it picks the newest kept image older than the running one, so calling it twice goes back two builds. With to, it uses that tag, a timestamp or prev. Before switching, it tags the running image prev, so prev always names the image that ran before the current one and rollback(host, 'prev') undoes the last deploy or rollback. A rollback moves only latest and prev: the running image keeps its timestamp, so rollback(host, to=<its tag>) returns to it after any number of rollbacks. vpseasy 0.0.25 and earlier tagged the replaced image undo; that tag is no longer written or read. The restart is docker compose up -d --no-build --force-recreate for the one service, so Compose uses the retagged image and does not build.
A rollback restores the image and nothing else. Files that sync copied to the server, such as the Compose file, the Caddyfile and bind-mounted folders, stay as the last deploy left them, and so do volumes and databases. The next deploy builds from your source again and keeps the rolled-back image like any other.

class FakeDocker:
    'A stand-in server: the commands `run_ssh` sends read and change a table of images, with their build times, and their tags.'
    def __init__(self, tags=None):
        self.tags, self.cmds, self.kw, self.n = dict(tags or {}), [], [], 0
        self.imgs = {i: '' for i in self.tags.values()}
    def __call__(self, host, *cmds, **kw):
        self.kw.append(kw); out = []
        for c in cmds:
            self.cmds.append(c); w = c.replace("'", '').split()
            if c.startswith('docker image inspect'):
                i = self.tags.get(w[5], w[5] if w[5] in self.imgs else '')
                out.append(self.imgs.get(i, '') if 'Created' in w[4] else i)
            elif c.startswith('docker image ls'): out += [f'{t.split(":")[1]} {i}' for t, i in self.tags.items() if t.split(':')[0] == w[3]]
            elif c.startswith('docker image prune'): self.imgs = {i: t for i, t in self.imgs.items() if i in self.tags.values()}
            elif c.startswith('docker tag'): self.tags[w[3]] = self.tags.get(w[2], w[2])
            elif c.startswith('docker rmi'): [self.tags.pop(t) for t in w[2:] if ':' in t]
            elif c.startswith('ls '): out.append(w[1])
            elif '--build' in c:
                self.n += 1; i = self.tags['app-app:latest'] = f'sha256:new{self.n}'
                self.imgs[i] = f'2026-10-{10+self.n:02d}T00:00:00.123456789Z'
        return '\n'.join(out)

    finally: g.update(o)

After a deploy
wait_http asks for url until it answers 200, up to tries times, poll seconds apart, and returns whether it did. Use it after deploy, before anything that needs the new version to be live, such as purging a CDN cache. ua sets the User-Agent: Cloudflare refuses some library agents, so give it a name of your own. text:
Docker Compose helpers
Most small web apps deployed with vpseasy run as the same group of containers. There is the app itself, Caddy as the web server in front of it, and usually a cloudflared container that connects to a Cloudflare tunnel, so the server needs no open web ports. They share a network called web, and Caddy keeps its certificates and settings in two named volumes, caddy_data and caddy_config. caddy_stack writes that Compose file in one call.
It takes the domain and a Dockerfile object from dockeasy, such as fasthtml_app(). It saves the Dockerfile, Caddyfile and docker-compose.yml into root, or into the current directory when root is not given, and returns the Compose object. vols are container directories whose contents should stay on the server’s disk. vols_to_binds turns each into a bind mount from a folder of the same name beside the Compose file, so /app/data is stored in ./data. The app reads environment variables from env_file, .env by default. cloudflared=False leaves the tunnel out and makes Caddy listen on ports 80 and 443. conf puts the Caddyfile somewhere else, and other keyword arguments go to dockeasy’s caddy_svc, for example email= or dns=.
app_kw, caddy_kw and cloudflared_kw add settings to one service each, such as mem_limit='3g' or init=True. A volumes list in them is added to the service’s own volumes rather than replacing them, so caddy_kw=dict(volumes=['./static:/srv/static:ro']) lets Caddy serve files from the deploy folder. Pass your own dockeasy Caddyfile as caddyfile to write it instead of the one built from the options, or write_caddyfile=False to leave the Caddyfile alone. Without conf, the Caddyfile sits in root beside the Compose file and is mounted as ./Caddyfile, so the stack works wherever root is. The litestream argument is covered in the next section.
The second cell shows the Compose file for a FastHTML app with one data volume.

title: core
text:
Litestream
Litestream copies every change to a SQLite database into an S3-compatible storage bucket, and can restore the database from that copy. The bucket can come from Lightsail.bucket, AWS S3 or Cloudflare R2.
litestream_conf writes Litestream’s config file and returns its text. dbs are absolute paths inside the container. If you pass vols, each database must sit inside one of them, or the Litestream container would not see it. Each database is stored at <prefix>/<db path> in the bucket, so two databases with the same file name do not collide. Litestream reads the access key from LITESTREAM_ACCESS_KEY_ID and LITESTREAM_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, which go in .env. The format was tested against litestream/litestream:0.5 (v0.5.17). Litestream ignores config keys it does not recognise without any warning.
litestream_svc returns the arguments for a Litestream service in Compose.svc(). It mounts the app’s volumes and the config file, and runs replicate unless you give another command.
You will rarely call either directly. caddy_stack(..., litestream=dict(dbs=..., bucket=..., endpoint=..., region=..., prefix=...)) writes the config and adds the services. A one-shot litestream-restore service runs restore -if-db-not-exists -if-replica-exists, which restores a database only when the file is missing and a copy exists in the bucket. The app waits for it to finish successfully, so a fresh server gets its data back before the app can create an empty database. The long-running litestream service starts after the app. With more than one database there is one restore service for each.
